intro16: The sensory pathways documented in the database suggest how the nervous system uses feedback from the legs to coordinate movement. To simulate what those pathways contribute, it is possible to combine a neural circuit model with the mechanical model of the body it controls. The circuit activates muscles, their forces move the joints, and the resulting changes in muscle stretch and load feed back to the circuit and shape its next commands. The robot’s artificial muscles differ from human muscles in how much force they produce and where they pull on the skeleton. A circuit that coordinates the legs of the human model will therefore produce a different movement in the robot model, and that movement will change the sensory feedback the circuit receives. To measure the effect of the mechanics, I wanted to repeat the same experiment on both models with the controller held fixed. I also wanted to test changes to the controller while keeping the mechanical model fixed. Our first neuromechanical model ran slowly, and we tuned its controller by hand, making a series of these comparisons impractical. I therefore developed tools to build circuits graphically, automate their tuning, and run those comparisons on a human musculoskeletal model and on models built from our robot's mechanical design (Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}). With human movement as a reference, the new system can simulate how changing a sensory connection or moving an artificial muscle attachment affects a mechanical model's coordination.
